assessment.nobel_worthiness: Foundational work formalising the political economy of trade protection (the 'protection for sale' framework) and, jointly, the theory of innovation, growth and trade. It reshaped how economists think about why trade policy departs from efficiency and gave a disciplined toolkit that is still used in applied work.
assessment.attribution: The Grossman-Helpman partnership is clearly the core of the contribution, with a long and tightly coupled joint record. The two-name credit fits well. Related contributions by others in the political economy of trade, such as Baldwin and Rodrik, are secondary to the joint framework.
assessment.maturity: Core results date from the early 1990s, so they have had decades of confirmation, empirical testing and extension. The growth-and-trade strand is complemented by the recently recognised work on innovation-led growth. Timing is not a constraint.
uncertainties: How the Committee weighs the political-economy-of-trade strand against the growth strand and against prior trade recognition (Krugman, 2008).
Empirical support for the protection-for-sale equilibrium is mixed, with estimated structural parameters that are sensitive to specification.
Helpman also appears on another ballot item, which complicates a prize design that sets the lines against each other.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation and dynamic oligopoly models turned industrial organisation into a quantitative, policy-relevant field. They underpin merger review, antitrust analysis and the measurement of market power across many industries and fields. The methodological reach is very broad and the real-world use is large.
assessment.attribution: The core is the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand framework, with Pakes also central to dynamic models (Ericson-Pakes). Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made important adjacent contributions, but the list is long, so a three-person limit forces hard choices about credit.
assessment.maturity: BLP (1995) and related methods have thirty years of use, replication and refinement, with extensive validation in applied work. The field is well established and the contribution is recognised as durable.
uncertainties: Which of Bresnahan, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn best represents the central idea within a three-name limit.
Persistent debate about identification and the credibility of structural assumptions relative to design-based approaches.
As an industrial-organisation economist I may weigh this field's importance more heavily than the broader Committee.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based account of technology and labour demand and the China-shock evidence on trade-induced local labour-market adjustment changed both academic and policy debate on inequality, polarisation and the distributional costs of trade. The empirical designs are widely emulated and the policy influence is large.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the central figures of the China-shock line. Autor is also central to the task and polarisation literature, alongside Acemoglu (recognised in 2024) and Katz. Katz's long-running contributions overlap but fall outside a three-name credit.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock papers (2013 onward) have a decade of follow-up, though some conclusions are still being refined in light of later evidence. The tasks work has deeper roots. Timing is plausible but not overdue.
uncertainties: Robustness of the shift-share identification and the persistence of effects have been debated.
Overlap with the 2024 recognition of technology and institutions, which may affect how the Committee frames the contribution.
Whether Katz should be included in place of one of the named trade economists.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The intertemporal approach to the current account and open-economy macroeconomics ('New Open Economy Macroeconomics', the 'Redux' model), together with the exchange-rate disconnect and related puzzles, is a pillar of modern international macroeconomics. It shaped central bank and IMF analysis and teaching.
assessment.attribution: The textbook and the Redux paper credit Obstfeld and Rogoff strongly. Others, such as Sachs, Dornbusch and Gopinath, built on or adjacent to the framework. The puzzles line has several originators, so attribution of the puzzles is less clean than for the framework.
assessment.maturity: The framework dates from the 1990s, and the puzzles remain partly unresolved, which is both a mark of relevance and a limit on confirmation. The model has been extended in many directions.
uncertainties: Several of the puzzles are unresolved, so the contribution is a research agenda rather than a settled result.
Rogoff also appears on another ballot item, which affects how a combined prize might be structured.
Empirical relevance of the Redux model's price-setting assumptions is limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Systematic integration of political institutions (electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity) into economic analysis, with testable implications for fiscal policy and public goods. It created the modern field of political economics, linking theory and empirical evidence across countries.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are clearly central through their joint program and book. Besley's related work on state capacity and accountability is a separate but closely allied contribution, which makes a three-person credit natural but not certain.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with twenty-five to thirty years of development and a large dependent literature. The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may affect how the Committee views the closeness of topics.
uncertainties: Possible perception of overlap with the 2024 institutions prize.
Empirical identification in cross-country electoral-rule comparisons is contested.
One member of the group has a close institutional link to the Committee, which may be a conflict. I note this without adjudicating it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Construction of long-run top-income and wealth series from tax data and the measurement of offshore wealth transformed empirical work on inequality and brought distributional questions to the centre of public debate. The data contribution is substantial and the influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit divides between data and measurement (Piketty-Saez, Zucman) and interpretive claims about capital and growth. The measurement work is the most solid base for a prize. Atkinson, who pioneered related historical income measurement, has died, which limits earlier lines of credit.
assessment.maturity: Core income series date from the early 2000s, but the capital-accumulation interpretation and offshore-wealth estimates remain contested, and revisions have been argued. The impact is evident, but confirmation is incomplete for some claims.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over the treatment of tax data, imputation and wealth capitalisation.
Whether the Committee would reward measurement and data construction relative to identified causal results.
Policy-contested terrain may raise the bar for consensus.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reoriented trade theory and empirics around firms, with implications for the gains from trade, productivity and market structure. The framework is close to the standard workhorse of modern trade analysis and links well to industrial organisation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extended it to exports versus foreign direct investment. Redding's contributions on quantitative spatial and trade models follow the framework. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important antecedents and could deserve credit.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation, though the framework refines rather than overturns the older models. The empirical facts on exporter premia were found earlier and independently.
uncertainties: Melitz's contribution is a single central paper, which may be seen as narrower than a prize usually reflects.
Strong overlap with other trade ballot items and with Helpman's credit on B001.
Credit overlap with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who established the exporter facts and related models.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Measurement of intergenerational mobility and place effects using population administrative data opened a data-intensive, policy-relevant line of work on opportunity, neighbourhoods and tax and social-insurance design. The scale of the data and the shaping of policy debate are notable.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the dominant figure in the program, with Hendren central to the place-effects work and Friedman and Katz also credited. A tight credit would reasonably focus on Chetty and one or two collaborators, but that choice is debatable and the collective nature of the team complicates it.
assessment.maturity: The central papers are from the 2010s onwards, so the findings are comparatively recent. Replication and longer-run follow-up on causal neighbourhood effects are still developing, which makes timing earlier than for the other items I rank above.
uncertainties: Relative youth of the work and incomplete long-run confirmation.
Debate over the causal interpretation of place-effect estimates and the sensitivity to specification.
Credit allocation across a large, collaborative research group.
